replies.author: @lucca_lee
replies.text:
The price Thailand has paid to avoid war is enormous, but hardly anyone ever talks about it. Thailand used to control a much larger territory, including numerous tributary states. Its sphere of influence was once considerably larger than the country we see on the map today, in some ways nearly twice its current size. But Thailand eventually had to give up much of that territory. Rather than fight the colonial powers to the bitter end, the Siamese government often chose to negotiate, pay financial compensation, sign treaties and make territorial concessions to France and England. Think about the economic cost and how difficult that decision must have been. Choosing not to fight goes against the instincts of many people, especially when they see territory being taken away. Burma chose to fight the British and ultimately lost its independence altogether. Siam took a different approach: it gradually surrendered its outlying territories while preserving its political independence and core territory only fight if neccesery to show the strength if anyone wann invest to conquer Thailand the price wont be cheap as for is some kind of investment the west know when to approuch and when not to, while also Thailabd seeking new diplomatic relationships with other European powers.
Then came World War II. Thailand initially declared neutrality, but Japan invaded because it wanted to use Thai territory as a route into Burma. The Thai government eventually sided with Japan, partly in the hope of recovering territories previously lost to Britain and France. Thailand did regain some of those territories, but only for a few years. When Japan lost the war, Thailand had to give them back to Britain and France. Meanwhile, Allied forces repeatedly bombed Thai cities and infrastructure. This is a real part of Thai history, but it's something Thailand rarely talks about in detail cause it not sound good to Thailand as well of being a sneaky nation. The Thai government also had to shoulder much of the burden of rebuilding the country after the war by it own money. Afterwards, the US offered assistance, but it came with strategic expectations, including allowing American military facilities in Thailand (for Vietnam war). Thailand didn't have much room to manoeuvre politically at that point. Although this postwar arrangement helped prevent Britain and France from imposing even harsher consequences, Thailand still had to pay war reparations to the Allies, largely in the form of agricultural goods. The country was extremely poor at the time. Even agricultural products that could have been sold abroad to generate revenue, or kept to feed the domestic population, had to be handed over as reparations. If you look at Thailand's GDP figures during that period, you'll see how economically weak the country was, despite not having experienced a prolonged war on its own soil. People sometimes wonder why Thailand didn't build on the wealth of its ancient kingdoms, which had once been major trading centres connecting East and West. But historical wealth doesn't automatically carry over into a modern economy. Much of that political and economic power had already disappeared long before modern Thailand began developing. This is also part of the reason Thailand started from a relatively weak economic position compared with countries like the Philippines. The Philippines and Vietnam had colonial-era economic structures that contributed to their early modern economies, although their colonial experiences were very different. Vietnam also received substantial support from the Soviet Union, which was one of the world's two superpowers at the time. Thailand, meanwhile, found itself in a difficult position after the Vietnam War. When the Americans withdrew following their defeat, Thailand could no longer rely on the same level of American military presence and support. It were left facing a very different regional security situation, including a powerful Vietnamese military presence in neighbouring Cambodia. Fortunately for Thailand, China's invasion of Vietnam in 1979 changed the regional balance and forced Vietnam to reconsider its strategic priorities otherwise Vietnam + Laos + Cambodia could have attacked Thailand directly, well after all what Thailand did to them in the past I would understand why they choose to so do. The cold war proxies also effect Thailand, if you have heard of Communist Domino the fall stop at Thailand and it wasnt for free it with tons of money spend to stop ot otherwise if could have successfull spread through the whole region.

There's another interesting aspect of Thailand's relationship with Japan. Unlike countries that experienced brutal Japanese occupation and mass atrocities, Thailand's wartime experience was more complicated. Thailand initially resisted the Japanese landings, and soldiers on both sides were killed before the Thai government agreed to cooperate. That initial resistance, along with Thailand's subsequent political decisions, may have contributed to Japan treating Thailand differently from some other occupied Asian countries.

Thailand wasn't simply obedient to Japan either. It maintained its own political interests and some room for manoeuvre throughout the war. Later, Japan became one of the most important foreign investors in Thailand, helping drive the country's industrial development. In my opinion, this postwar economic relationship was a much more important turning point than people often realise.

That's the real point I'm trying to make: most countries in Southeast Asia started out relatively poor when the modern global economy took shape. Their economic paths were shaped by very different historical circumstances, political decisions, foreign assistance and investment. You can't simply compare their GDP figures today without considering what each country had to go through to get there.

That's just how percentages work. For example, let's say Person A has $1,000 and earns a 3% return, which gives them $30. Meanwhile, Person B has only $500 but earns a 5% return, giving them $25. Even though B has a higher growth rate, A still makes more money in absolute terms. If this continues, B will struggle to catch up unless they consistently achieve a significantly higher return. In this example, B would need to earn more than 6% while A earns 3% to start closing the gap. It's basic math.
A: $1,000 × 3% = $30 → $1,030
B: $500 × 5% = $25 → $525
B needs a 6% return just to match A's $30 gain in the first year. To actually catch up with A's total balance over time, B needs to outperform A by a sufficient margin consistently. The only country can do this and will surpass Thailand is Vietnam. the PH is a long long way to go.

replies.text:
Thai government is as corupt as the PH but the model of Thai corupt is more like allow people to do what ever they want as long as they keep paying under table not that they block anyone from doing business it aint fair but people still survive .... Having good relations with China doesn't necessarily benefit Thailand economically as much as people might think. Thai products simply can't compete with Chinese products in many sectors. big Thai company can complete with anyone but ordinary SME ... Not so much. Good relations between the two governments have also facilitated massive trade between the countries, but the trade balance is heavily in China's favour, with Thailand importing far more from China than it exports. On the other hand, Thailand is fortunate that it doesn't share a border with China. That would make our situation considerably more complicated. We already have enough problems dealing with our neighbours: Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia and even Malaysia.Thailand actually spends a considerable amount on its military compared with the Philippines, partly because of the security challenges along its borders. I honestly can't imagine how much more complicated things would become if China were added to the equation. By the way, Cambodia is still building bunkers along the border, almost as if it's preparing to try its luck again. Along the Myanmar border, the Burmese military is fighting its own ethnic armed groups, and there have been instances of bombs and military activity spilling over into Thai territory. The Thai military has even had to deploy F-16s to patrol the border area.
Then there's the far south. The three southernmost provinces have a predominantly Malay Muslim population, and there has been a long-running separatist insurgency there, with bombings and security incidents occurring regularly, sometimes almost every week. These aren't exactly secrets. They're regularly reported in Thai news, but foreign media don't seem particularly interested in covering these issues, so you might not hear much about them. My point is that Thailand already has plenty of security challenges to deal with than people may realize, the last incident with Cambodia, people had to evacuate hundred thousand of them out of tye border for a month with tona military upgrade later on.

​@LanghangGan-d2k5cManila is even smaller than a third of Bangkok. Even if you combined all the developed areas of the Philippines, the total area would still be tiny. A few kilometers away, everything is underdeveloped.
Bangkok's streets and sidewalks are clean now. How many years ago were you in Sukhumvit? And Thailand isn't just Sukhumvit; there's Phahonyothin Road, Victory Monument, Siam Square, Asoke Intersection, Silom, Sathorn, and Lumphini Park – all developed. The sidewalks are wide and spacious, and the BTS and MRT systems, with a total length of over 280 kilometers, are interconnected throughout Bangkok. Compare that to Manila's city trains, which are smelly, hot, and dirty, and have very short stretches. While Bangkok's power grid might seem messy, it has improved significantly in many areas. Manila's power lines are only good in short stretches near buildings; the rest is even worse than Bangkok. The streets are filled with honking horns, making a deafening noise like in India.
